action_criteria.expected_evidence: Serum anti-GluN1 IgG positive (titer 1:160), read with the CSF; sodium normal; CK 200 U/L; thyroid function and thyroid antibodies negative
action_criteria.label: Obtain the serum work-up: blood count, chemistry, thyroid function and antibodies, HIV, beta-hCG and a cell-based serum anti-GluN1 IgG assay read together with the CSF result
action_criteria.rationale: Screens metabolic, endocrine, infectious and pregnancy-related contributors, gives the CK baseline after olanzapine and pairs the serum antibody with the decisive CSF assay.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Subtle left medial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity without restricted diffusion, hemorrhage or enhancement; no structural or demyelinating lesion
action_criteria.label: Obtain contrast-enhanced brain MRI to exclude HSV encephalitis, structural lesions and overlapping demyelination; a normal MRI does not exclude anti-NMDAR encephalitis
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes HSV encephalitis, structural lesions and overlapping demyelination before LP; it is normal in most patients and does not confirm the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Lymphocytic pleocytosis (18 cells/uL), elevated IgG index and CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands; HSV-1/2 PCR negative; CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titer 1:32)
action_criteria.label: Analyze CSF for cells, protein and glucose, oligoclonal bands or IgG index, HSV PCR and a cell-based IgG anti-GluN1 assay
action_criteria.rationale: The CSF anti-GluN1 cell-based assay is the decisive test (Graus 2016 definite criteria), and HSV PCR addresses the infectious mimic that must not be missed.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Diffuse slowing with bifrontal rhythmic delta, delta with superimposed beta short of extreme delta brush, and one brief left temporal seizure
action_criteria.label: Obtain an EEG for encephalopathic and epileptiform abnormalities, including extreme delta brush
action_criteria.rationale: An abnormal EEG is one of the Graus 2016 supporting findings, and the witnessed behavioral arrests need electrographic characterization.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No adnexal mass; polycystic ovaries with a simple left follicle
action_criteria.label: Screen for an ovarian teratoma with pelvic and abdominal ultrasound
action_criteria.rationale: Women of reproductive age carry the highest teratoma risk; tumor removal is part of first-line treatment.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Seizure burden and evolution of the background over 24 hours or more
action_criteria.label: Escalate to continuous EEG to quantify seizure burden while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist
action_criteria.rationale: The routine EEG captured a seizure during a behavioral arrest and the arrests recur, so a 45-minute record underestimates the seizure burden.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Olanzapine to be stopped (D2 antagonist intolerance, seizure threshold); steroid hyperglycemia on metformin
action_criteria.label: Check the patient's medications against the drugs the acute plan needs (acyclovir, corticosteroids, IVIG, antiseizure medication)
action_criteria.rationale: She has been on olanzapine for 5 days, and the check guides its withdrawal and the choice of a benzodiazepine for agitation.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1-2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
required_recommendations: Start IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for the antibody result once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange (5 to 7 exchanges).

Pelvic ultrasound shows no tumor: repeat pelvic imaging (MRI or transvaginal ultrasound) if the response to immunotherapy is poor or the disease relapses, and continue tumor surveillance during follow-up.
Treat seizures with an antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam or lacosamide; avoid valproate in a woman able to become pregnant; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.
Admit to a neurology ward with seizure precautions and continuous cardiac monitoring.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, escalate to rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide; discuss fertility preservation before cyclophosphamide.
Treat agitation and insomnia with benzodiazepines (lorazepam) first; stop olanzapine and monitor CK and temperature.
Neurology-led care with psychiatry for behavioral management.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

differential.key_features: CSF HSV-1/2 PCR negative three weeks after onset; MRI without hemorrhage or restricted diffusion; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.

differential.diagnosis: Other antibody-mediated encephalitis (anti-LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B or AMPA receptor)
differential.key_features: Serum neuronal-surface panel negative (LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, DPPX) and onconeural antibodies negative; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.
The generalized seizure, left temporal electroclinical seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, heart-rate lability and CSF pleocytosis with oligoclonal bands are not explained by a primary psychosis.

Maternal aunt has SLE and ANA is 1:80 speckled, a low titer common in healthy people; no rash, arthritis, serositis, cytopenia or renal involvement, and the CSF anti-GluN1 result accounts for the syndrome.

differential.diagnosis: Drug-induced movement disorder, NMS or serotonin syndrome (olanzapine, sertraline)
differential.key_features: Olanzapine 5 mg for 5 days and a recent sertraline increase, but temperature 37.7 C, CK 200 U/L, mild tone increase without lead-pipe rigidity and no clonus; the psychiatric change, seizures and CSF findings began or exist independently of these drugs.

key_clinical_evidence: Three weeks of subacute behavioral and cognitive change with insomnia, speech disturbance (pressured speech alternating with reduced output), seizures, orofacial dyskinesias and heart-rate lability: five of the six Graus 2016 groups.
CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titer 1:32) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016); serum positive (1:160) is read with the CSF.

MRI shows only subtle left medial temporal FLAIR signal without restricted diffusion or hemorrhage; MRI is normal or non-specific in about two thirds of patients and here excludes HSV encephalitis and structural causes.
EEG shows diffuse slowing, delta with superimposed beta short of extreme delta brush and left temporal seizures; extreme delta brush, when present, supports but does not establish the diagnosis.
Pelvic ultrasound shows no tumor; tumor surveillance continues, and olanzapine exposure must be stopped because of neuroleptic intolerance in this disease.
Earlier immunotherapy and tumor removal are associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF pleocytosis alongside the psychiatric change mandate exclusion of anti-NMDAR encephalitis before a psychiatric diagnosis is accepted.
red_herrings.data_point: Acute psychiatric presentation (insomnia, paranoia, emotional lability) in a young woman with an anxiety disorder, treated as anxiety and then as first-episode psychosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on a primary psychiatric diagnosis (first-episode psychosis, brief psychotic disorder) and delays neurologic workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: NMS requires antipsychotic exposure with lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia and markedly elevated CK; despite 5 days of olanzapine, a CK of 200 U/L with temperature 37.7 C reflects seizures and dyskinesias, though the olanzapine should still be stopped.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Raises concern for neuroleptic malignant syndrome after olanzapine when combined with dyskinesias and increased tone.

alternatives: Lorazepam IV or oral as needed for agitation

contraindications: Haloperidol and other high-potency D2 antagonists: class warning for severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions in suspected autoimmune encephalitis.
interactions: Olanzapine: D2 antagonist; lowers the seizure threshold and can worsen dyskinesias and rigidity; severe neuroleptic intolerance is reported in suspected autoimmune encephalitis. Discontinue and use a benzodiazepine for agitation.
Olanzapine with sertraline: additive QTc effect is small; check the ECG before any further QT-prolonging drug.
Sertraline: serotonergic; recent dose increase. Monitor for serotonin toxicity (clonus, hyperthermia) and hyponatremia.
Metformin with high-dose methylprednisolone: corticosteroid hyperglycemia; monitor capillary glucose.
Albuterol with high-dose methylprednisolone: additive hypokalemia; monitor potassium.
Norethindrone (progestin-only pill): no clinically relevant interaction with levetiracetam, acyclovir or corticosteroids.
Acyclovir: no interaction with the current medicines; dose by renal function and maintain hydration.

anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis diagnosi.query: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis diagnosis and treatment

results.finding: Definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis requires one or more of six major symptom groups and IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies, with CSF testing included; probable disease requires four groups (or three with a teratoma) of rapid onset plus an abnormal EEG or CSF pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands.
results.source: Graus F et al. Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404

results.finding: All patients had antibodies in CSF, whereas about 14% were negative in serum; CSF titers related more closely to outcome than serum titers.
results.source: Gresa-Arribas N et al. Lancet Neurol 2014;13:167-177

results.finding: 38% had a tumor, mostly ovarian teratoma; 53% improved within 4 weeks of first-line immunotherapy or tumor removal; second-line rituximab or cyclophosphamide after first-line failure was associated with better outcome; 81% had mRS 0-2 at 24 months.
results.source: Titulaer MJ et al. Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165

results.finding: Extreme delta brush was found in 7 of 23 adults with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis and was associated with a more prolonged illness.
Severe intolerance to antipsychotics (rigidity, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions) was frequent in patients with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis who received them.
results.source: Lejuste F et al. Neurol Neuroimmunol Neuroinflamm 2016;3:e280

anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis diagnosi.summary: Published criteria and cohort data on anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: definite diagnosis rests on CSF IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies; first-line immunotherapy and tumor removal are followed by second-line agents when there is no response.

patient.history_present_illness: This 33-year-old right-handed woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband after three weeks of progressive behavioral and cognitive decline, culminating in a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure earlier today. Her husband reports that approximately three weeks ago she began having difficulty sleeping, waking multiple times per night and sometimes not sleeping at all. He initially attributed this to work stress as she had recently taken on additional responsibilities at her school. Within a few days, she became increasingly irritable and emotionally labile, crying without clear provocation and snapping at her students, which was highly unusual for her. She saw her primary care physician ten days ago, who attributed the symptoms to worsening anxiety and increased her sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg daily. Despite this, her symptoms progressed. Over the following week, she became increasingly confused, forgetting conversations from minutes earlier and misplacing household items. She began expressing paranoid thoughts, telling her husband that her coworkers were conspiring against her and that hidden cameras were placed in their home. Her husband took her to an urgent psychiatric evaluation five days ago, where she was prescribed olanzapine 5 mg nightly for possible first-episode psychosis. However, her mental status continued to deteriorate. Three days ago, her husband noticed involuntary repetitive lip movements and odd hand gestures that she did not seem aware of. Yesterday, she was unable to prepare a simple meal and appeared disoriented within their home. This morning, her husband witnessed her develop sudden bilateral arm stiffening followed by generalized shaking lasting approximately 60 seconds with tongue biting and urinary incontinence, followed by 20 minutes of post-ictal confusion. Emergency medical services were called and she was transported to the emergency department. Upon arrival, she was intermittently agitated and confused, unable to provide a coherent history. She has had no recent travel, no known sick contacts, no tick bites, and no new medications other than those prescribed in the past two weeks. Her husband denies any recreational drug use.

neurological_exam.additional: Intermittent perioral dyskinesias and stereotyped hand movements observed during examination. One episode of sudden behavioral arrest lasting approximately 10 seconds with staring and lip automatisms, followed by confusion, witnessed during the encounter. Heart rate noted to fluctuate between 85 and 118 bpm during the 45-minute evaluation without clear precipitant.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing performed inconsistently; mild bilateral dysmetria noted but reliability is questionable given encephalopathy. Heel-to-shin not assessed due to inability to cooperate.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm, equal and reactive bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact. Subtle decreased nasolabial fold on the left, though cooperation limits reliable assessment. Hearing intact to finger rub bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without atrophy or fasciculations. Intermittent perioral dyskinesias with repetitive lip movements noted during examination.
neurological_exam.gait: Unsteady, wide-based gait with tendency to veer to the right. Required two-person assist. Tandem gait not attempted.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but confused and intermittently agitated. Oriented to self only; unable to state the date, month, or location. Speech is fluent but tangential with occasional paraphasic errors. Able to follow simple one-step commands but fails multi-step instructions. Intermittent pressured speech alternating with periods of decreased verbal output. Short-term memory significantly impaired: recalls 1 of 3 objects at 5 minutes. Attention is poor; unable to spell WORLD backwards or perform serial 7s. Intermittent paranoid ideation, stating the nursing staff is trying to harm her.
neurological_exam.motor: Tone mildly increased in bilateral upper extremities, more pronounced on the right. Strength grossly 4+/5 throughout, limited by poor cooperation and fluctuating attention. No definite focal weakness. Occasional stereotyped hand movements bilaterally, described as pill-rolling and finger-wiggling.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 3+ bilaterally (brisk), Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws to pain symmetrically in all extremities. Detailed sensory testing unreliable due to encephalopathy and poor cooperation.
